stem: A client receiving pembrolizumab asks why the nurse repeatedly asks about new cough, diarrhea, rash, fatigue, jaundice, and endocrine-type symptoms. Which explanation is most accurate?

options.A: Pembrolizumab activates antitumor immune responses by blocking PD-1 signaling, but this can also produce immune-mediated inflammation or injury in normal organs and tissues, sometimes during treatment or after it ends.
options.B: Pembrolizumab suppresses the entire immune system, so these questions are mainly intended to detect ordinary opportunistic infections caused by global immunosuppression.
options.C: Pembrolizumab affects only the tumor site, so symptoms involving the lungs, bowel, liver, skin, or endocrine glands are unrelated to treatment.
options.D: Immune-mediated adverse reactions occur only during the infusion itself and cannot begin after the infusion or after treatment has been completed.

rationale: Current FDA labeling identifies pembrolizumab as a PD-1-blocking antibody. Blocking the PD-1 pathway can enhance T-cell antitumor activity but can also cause severe or fatal immune-mediated adverse reactions in essentially any organ system. The current Medication Guide warns that the immune system may attack normal organs and tissues, that more than one immune-mediated problem may occur at the same time, and that these problems may begin during treatment or after treatment has ended. Therefore, A is correct. B incorrectly describes global immune suppression, C denies multisystem toxicity, and D incorrectly limits toxicity to the infusion period.
educational_objective: Explain that pembrolizumab's PD-1 immune activation can cause multisystem immune-mediated adverse reactions that may occur during or after treatment and therefore require ongoing symptom surveillance.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / U.S. Food and Drug Administration labeling via DailyMed
source_document_title: KEYTRUDA (pembrolizumab) — Official Prescribing Information and Medication Guide
source_locator: Section 12.1, Mechanism of Action: pembrolizumab is a PD-1-blocking antibody that releases PD-1-mediated inhibition of the immune response and enhances antitumor responses. Section 5.1, Severe and Fatal Immune-Mediated Adverse Reactions: immune-mediated adverse reactions can be severe or fatal, can occur in any organ system or tissue, and may occur during or after treatment. Medication Guide: KEYTRUDA may cause the immune system to attack normal organs/tissues; multiple problems can occur simultaneously and may occur after treatment ends.
source_claim_supported: Directly supports PD-1 immune activation as the therapeutic mechanism and the related possibility of severe multisystem immune-mediated adverse reactions during or after pembrolizumab treatment.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies → Adverse Effects/Immunotherapy: understand medication action, monitor for multisystem immune-mediated toxicity, and educate clients to report new or worsening symptoms during and after therapy.
blueprint_topic: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — pembrolizumab immune-mediated adverse reactions
correction_summary: Converted the source's broad checkpoint-inhibitor class item into a pembrolizumab-specific question using the current June 2026 KEYTRUDA label. The final item preserves the mechanism-to-toxicity relationship but avoids assuming that every checkpoint inhibitor has identical labeling, incidence, or management rules.

audit_findings.source_authority: Current official FDA KEYTRUDA prescribing information and Medication Guide via DailyMed.
audit_findings.currentness: The selected KEYTRUDA label was updated June 24, 2026 and includes May/June 2026 warning/indication changes.

claim_by_claim.stem: The multisystem symptom examples map to known immune-mediated toxicities involving lung, GI tract, liver, skin, endocrine organs and other tissues.
claim_by_claim.A: Correct because PD-1 blockade enhances antitumor immunity and can trigger immune-mediated injury of normal organs during or after therapy.
claim_by_claim.B: Incorrect because pembrolizumab is not described as global immune-system suppression; its mechanism releases PD-1 inhibitory signaling.
claim_by_claim.C: Incorrect because immune-mediated reactions can involve essentially any organ system rather than remaining localized to tumor tissue.
claim_by_claim.D: Incorrect because reactions may occur after treatment ends and are not limited to the infusion period.
claim_by_claim.rationale: Does not imply that every listed symptom is definitely immune-mediated; surveillance is required because alternative causes must also be considered clinically.
claim_by_claim.educational_objective: Specific to mechanism-linked symptom surveillance during/after pembrolizumab.

audit_findings.distractor_audit: B confuses immune activation with global suppression, C falsely localizes toxicity, and D falsely limits timing. Each is clinically meaningful and distinct.
audit_findings.ambiguity_and_second_answer: Only A matches both current mechanism and immune-mediated safety labeling.
audit_findings.cueing: All options explain why multisystem symptoms are monitored during immunotherapy.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies directly fits immunotherapy mechanism, client education, and adverse-effect monitoring.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited whether 'enhances immune system activity' is too broad. The final rationale specifies release of PD-1-mediated inhibition and enhanced T-cell antitumor response, preserving mechanistic precision without overclaiming generalized immune activation. No unresolved conflict remains.
